The manuscript by Hussain et al. reports data on the dynamics of MreB filaments in Bacillus subtilis cells with altered cell shape. Using an impressive array of in vivo and in vitro approaches, they convincingly show that MreB moves in the direction of the largest membrane curvature, i.e. along the short axis in rod-shape cells and with random orientation in spherical cells. This movement somehow directs cell wall synthesis and guides/reinforces rod shape formation. Interestingly, when spherical cells convert to rods, elongative growth starts at a ring at the base of a bulge that grows to form a new rod-shaped cell body. The authors propose a model according to which MreB movement functions to strengthen the cross-linkage of the cell wall peptidoglycan.

Although the work is an important addition to the field several points made by the authors should be toned down before the paper is published.

- While it is possible that MreB indeed affects PG crosslinks, the peptidoglycan (PG) analysis data have major flaws because:i) The authors do not use the appropriate strains and conditions to test if oriented MreB motion results in more cross-linked PG.ii) They did not use the appropriate methodology to determine the muropeptide composition (see specific comments below). Therefore, the authors cannot draw any conclusions from the data presented and they should remove the flawed PG analysis data and all conclusions/models based on these from the manuscript.

- Although MreB could be sufficient to generate rod shape, the data does not prove it and thus the title is an overstatement (as well as any issuing statement). The whole set of data gathered present very clear evidence that MreB aligned along the highest curvature and even bend liposomes because it prefers a sharp ~200nm ring structure to align with. But that does not mean it creates the shape, only that once there, it aligns with it. In fact, the experiments do not rule that there is not another factor in charge of creating the rod and that the resulting structure in turn recruits MreB. Perhaps, the absence of TagO, leading to the loss of rod shape despite an MreB-dependent oriented synthesis, suggests MreB may not be sufficient. Similarly, the authors do not refer to a paper from the Gitai group showing that rodZ mutants of E. coli are able to grow as rods without MreB motion. How does this work relate to their model? Is MreB-motion required in Bacillus for rod-shape maintenance?

- The assumption that MreB and Mbl are interchangeable is a big stretch. It is still unclear why B. subtilis have several paralogs and if they carry specific functions. Since the authors are bringing new insights on a critical feature of MreBs, it is important to show that this can be extend to both MreB and Mbl, without starting with such assumption. At the very least, they should stick to one and not go back and forth between both. For example, in Figure 2—video 1, it is not acceptable to show GFP-MreB as a control experiment but use Mbl-GFP in the tagO knockout. This is not the only example. Many experiments are performed with one or the other protein, the authors should either "fill the gaps" or justify rigorously the choice of a given fusion for a given experiment.

Specific comments:

1) Peptidoglycan:

1) Does the oriented MreB motion help to incorporate PG with normal composition/cross-linkage, and is therefore the PG composition/cross-linkage altered in spherical cells (Figure 6B, Supplementary Figure 6D)? They aimed to answer this question by analysing the total PG of cells harvested from an over-night culture (subsection “Muropeptide analysis”), which is a poor experiment for two reasons. First, it is known that newly incorporated PG changes its structure over time (PG maturation) resulting in significant changes in the muropeptide composition; not all of the later PG maturation steps may be affected by the motion of MreB. Hence, to answer the question requires to determine the composition of newly made PG just after its incorporation into the cell wall near the membrane (and guided by MreB motion), perhaps by analysing the structure of new PG made during a short pulse after the addition of a radioactive compound incorporating into PG. Second, an overnight culture of B. subtilis contains a complex and unknown mixture of growing and non-growing cells, lysing cells, lysed cells, sporulating cells and spores, and over-night cultures of rod-shaped or spherical cells might well differ in the degree of lysis, sporulation etc. The overall PG composition of such mixtures may be related to MreB motion only indirectly or not at all. In my view to answer the question would require to analyse the composition of nascent PG upon short labelling in exponentially growing cells.

Strain chosen for determining the composition of the PG. They used the tagO depletion strain called BEG300 (which also expressed a Gfp-MreB protein; why would they need this?). The strain is a poor choice because the depleted cells lack wall teichoic acid and are therefore more prone to autolysis (endogenous PG hydrolases are known to be affected by the presence of teichoic acids). Ideally, one would use round cells that do not differ in the teichoic acid content, to prevent uncontrolled cleavage by hydrolases which alters the muropeptide profile. That the round cells of the tagO depleted cells (from the overnight-cultures) suffered from uncontrolled PG hydrolase activity is readily seen from the data presented in Figure 6B and Supplementary Figure 6D: I am not aware of any muropeptide profile of a strain/mutant from a Gram-positive species with a cross-linkage of as low as 11%, as was determined here. This low cross-linkage must come from uncontrolled activity of autolysins because of the presence of the disaccharide tetrapeptide muropeptide (peak 3, Supplementary Figure 6D) that is not normally present in PG from Bacillus subtilis. This muropeptide originates from uncontrolled endopeptidase activity, degrading tetra-tri dimers to tetra and tri monomers, explaining both the low cross-linkage and the presence of tetra monomers. In my view this uncontrolled endopeptidase activity has nothing to do with the lack of orientation of the MreB motion, but is just a sign of extensive lysis of tagO depleted cells during over-night cultivation.

The PG isolation method used does not allow quantitative analysis of muropeptide composition. Remarkably, they wrote: "To prepare muropeptides from strain BEG300, a similar protocol was performed as reported previously (Atrih et al., 1999; Kuhner et al., 2014)". This statement is incorrect because both cited papers describe two very different PG isolation methods, and what they have used was the quick method by Kuhner et al., 2014 and not the method by Atrih et al., 1999. Importantly, only the Atrih method allows to isolate muropeptides for quantitative analysis. The Kuhner et al., 2014 reports a quicker and simpler method to isolate muropeptides to determine their structure, but for many reasons this method is not appropriate for quantitative determination of muropeptide composition. Indeed, the Kuhner paper does not claim that the new method is to determine the composition; they rather provided mass spectrometry data for the muropeptides isolated (from E. coli and S. aureus) but, rightly so, the Kuhner paper does not provide any quantitative data on the profiles they obtained. Hence, Hussain et al. should have used the Atrih method to isolate muropeptides for quantitative analysis.

Supplementary Figure 6D illustrates major problems of the data presented. The structures and many masses determined (as mentioned in the legend of Supplementary Figure 6D) are obviously erroneous: previous publications showed that the majority of the meso-Dap residues in the PG from B. subtilis are amidated, due to amidation of the lipid II precursor, but this modification is not seen in their muropeptide structures. The tetrasaccharide (with tetra-tri peptide) is split into 4 peaks (No. 4, 5, 6 and 7) with the same mass, with retention times that differ by almost 10 minutes, and the determined mass of 1795.8 is 3 Da off the theoretical mass of 1792.8 Da (H+ versions) of the B. subtilis tetra-tri muropeptide. The presence of 4 peaks and the discrepancy to the theoretical mass (which is too high considering the accuracy of current mass spectrometers) are not explained, but I conclude that the muropeptide patterns and masses presented in Supplementary Figure 6D and its legend are not consistent with what is known about PG from B. subtilis.

Another obvious mistake in the manuscript is the sentence: "Similar muropeptides were observed as previously reported for other Bacillus subtilis strains (Kuhner et al., 2014)". Although they cite Kuhner et al., 2014 in this way, they seem to be unaware that Kuhner et al., 2014 does not report any data on Bacillus subtilis muropeptides! In fact, the Kuhner et al. 2014 paper only reports data for muropeptides from E. coli and S. aureus.

2) Protoplasts:

Absence of CW synthesis in protoplast (subsection “MreB Aligns Within Round Cells and Protoplasts Forced into Rod Shape”, last paragraph): This experiment using WGA tagging to show the absence of PG is useless at two levels. The control is useless as it is, because it does not prove there is no CW, but fortunately, this is not required for the demonstration. Since the cells have been protoplasted, we know that most of the PG is gone, by definition. The purpose of this control is to check if residual PG, too thin or non-continuous (thus insufficient to counteract osmotic pressure and maintain shape) could still be present and serve as tracks. The problem is if there were residual PG strands, would the WGA staining be sensitive enough to detect traces of PG? In fairness, we do not know and it would be interesting to know what can be detected by this method. However, as it is, this experiment is not a good control and would require to first prove than it can detect such traces by checking cells containing decreasing quantities of CW in parallel to another more sensitive approach (HPLC?). Now, this control is not critical because if there are traces of PG, they will be present both in the rod and round sections of the protoplast and will not be sufficient to organize the movement of MreBs in round areas anyway. This control should be removed and the text should be toned down, since there is no certainty that "any structure within the cell wall" has been removed.

Average angular distributions compared between wt and protoplasts of various width (see the aforementioned paragraph). The authors report a broadening of the distribution with the increase of the imposed width. But Figure 3F legend says that the standard deviation SD +/- 35° at 4µ, thus not significantly broader than in wt cells (SD +/-34°). Also, it is noticeable that the average angles are not significantly different between the cells tested: 86° observed with 5µ protoplasts and 88° observed in the Wt (with SD > 30°). Thus, the numbers do not agree with the authors' description in text. Could this discrepancy come from the fact that averages may not fully reflects the changes and that a graphical representation of the distribution would be more appropriate? The >90° angles reported in the text and legend are puzzling. For example, the authors report 93° and 94° for 2µ width protoplasts with MreB and Mbl. The angle distribution so far (Figure 1 and 3) presented distributions ranging between 10 and 90°, thus not discriminating the direction of the pole that the patch is leaning to. It is therefore puzzling that the average numbers are here above 90°, hence now considering this direction. This is a bit misleading the values are very different from that observed in protoplast (81 and 86° at 4 and 5µ width) with wider shape, while in fact they are quite close.

3) WTA labeling:

WTA is uniformly distributed (Figure 6B). It does not seem completely uniform on the presented images, with accumulation in inward bending of the membrane. In fact, the increase in WTA is more convincing than the MreB accumulation presented in Figure 6B; Also, the assertion that the ligases move homogeneously in the membrane is not fully convincing. First, the cells in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C are too small for the reader to assert a lack of tracks for the Ligases (MIP). In fact, if a fraction of the population of ligases were interacting with MreB and move directionally, this could be easily missed with the MIP because of the bad S/N ratio. If the authors want to make this point (not critical for the whole story), single particle tracking would here be more appropriate to check for the absence of such a subpopulation.

results.result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about MreB, including its essentiality for rod shape, its structure as an actin homolog forming antiparallel double filaments, its ability to bend membranes, and its properties in B. subtilis where three paralogs co-polymerize and colocalize.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C3, C37-C43) represent well-established prior knowledge supported by multiple citations to the literature. They provide necessary context for the study and are appropriately referenced.

results.result: MreB and Mbl trajectories in B. subtilis are predominantly circumferential (mode at 90°) but broadly distributed (mean deviations of 34° and 26° respectively), with trajectories frequently crossing paths, indicating the sacculus lacks perfect order.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 and C61 are supported by quantitative trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1B-C with substantial sample sizes (n=1041 for MreB, n=1772 for Mbl). The crossing trajectories provide visual evidence against a perfectly ordered template.

results.result: Modulating TagO expression and Mg2+ levels allows controlled manipulation of cell shape from rods to spheres, with cell width increasing as TagO is depleted, and both parameters showing interdependence in determining the rod/sphere transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 and C73-C77 are well-supported by systematic experiments shown in Figure 1D-F with appropriate sample sizes and error bars. The Mg2+ dependence provides additional validation that the effects are related to cell wall rigidity rather than artifacts.

results.result: MreB motion is oriented circumferentially in rod-shaped cells but becomes isotropic in round cells, with quantitative analysis showing median angle differences of 26° in rods versus 42° in spheres (approaching the 45° expected for random orientation).
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C78-C81 represent a central finding supported by Figure 2A-B with substantial sample sizes. The quantitative metrics clearly distinguish oriented from isotropic motion, and the comparison to random trajectories strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: During Pbp2a/PbpH depletion, cells gradually widen and convert to spheres, with MreB motion remaining circumferential in rod-shaped cells but becoming unoriented in round cells, confirming that MreB orientation depends on cell shape rather than specific genetic perturbations.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by time-course experiments shown in Figure 2C-D. The gradual transition provides temporal resolution, and the observation that both GFP-MreB and GFP-Mbl show identical behavior strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: MreB motion remains oriented over a wide range of rod widths up to ~2 μm, beyond which orientation is lost as cells become spherical, suggesting that MreB orientation depends on differences in principal curvatures rather than absolute cell radius.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are supported by systematic analysis across different cell widths shown in Figure 2E. The identification of a critical width (~2 μm) where orientation is lost, corresponding to where cells become spherical, provides strong evidence for the curvature-based mechanism.

results.result: Externally imposing rod shape on TagO-depleted cells using microfluidic confinement restores circumferential MreB motion, demonstrating that MreB orientation is a direct response to cell shape rather than an artifact of genetic manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C92-C96 describe a critical control experiment shown in Figure 3A-C. The microfluidic confinement approach elegantly separates shape effects from genetic effects, and the restoration of oriented motion upon confinement provides strong causal evidence.

results.result: Rod-shaped cells grow significantly faster than spherical cells (doubling times of ~40 min vs ~53 min), and this growth advantage is restored when spherical cells are confined into rod shape, suggesting the effect is due to shape rather than other factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 and C133-C135 are supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C. The restoration of growth rate upon confinement and the Mg2+ dependence provide evidence that shape is the key factor.

results.result: MreB filaments orient circumferentially within protoplasts confined into rod shapes but remain unoriented in spherically confined protoplasts, demonstrating that orientation occurs independently of pre-existing cell wall or directional motion, with alignment becoming more disordered as rod width increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C99-C106 describe elegant protoplast experiments shown in Figure 3E-F. The absence of cell wall and directional motion eliminates potential confounding factors, and the width-dependent disorder (34° at 2 μm to 41° at 5 μm) supports the curvature-based mechanism.

results.result: Purified T. maritima MreB tubulates liposomes in vitro, with filaments orienting circumferentially in tubulated regions but randomly in spherical regions, and preferentially binding to inward (negative) curvatures, demonstrating that MreB filaments are intrinsically sufficient for curvature-dependent alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C107-C114 are supported by cryoEM data shown in Figure 4A-B. The in vitro reconstitution with purified protein eliminates cellular complexity, and the observation of orientation in tubes but not spheres provides strong evidence for an intrinsic curvature-sensing mechanism.

results.result: Biophysical modeling demonstrates that MreB filaments minimize energy when oriented along the direction of maximal curvature, with the energy penalty for misorientation exceeding thermal fluctuations, and this orientation is robust across biologically relevant parameter ranges and different osmotic pressure conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C115-C123 present modeling results shown in Figure 4E-G and detailed in Appendix 1. The modeling appropriately considers membrane deformation, filament bending, and osmotic pressure. The robustness analysis (Figure 4G) and qualitative agreement with experimental observations strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Rod shape is lost through continuous swelling without reversion, and can only be maintained when the cell wall is sufficiently rigid to resist osmotic pressure, with cells at intermediate TagO levels showing repeated cycles of rod formation and reversion to spheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5A and steady-state observations in Figure 1D,F. The unidirectional nature of the rod-to-sphere transition and the existence of intermediate states support the rigidity-based model.

results.result: Rod shape regenerates from spherical cells in a local, self-reinforcing manner, with rods emerging from small outward bulges that immediately begin rapid elongation, independent of cell division, suggesting bulge formation acts as the nucleating event.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 and C127-C132 are supported by recovery experiments shown in Figure 5B-D. The observation that bulge width matches emerging rod width, the independence from FtsZ, and the rapid elongation following bulge formation provide strong evidence for local nucleation.

results.result: Emerging rods exhibit oriented MreB motion from their initial formation while attached spherical cells show unoriented motion, with MreB transiently accumulating in rings at bulge necks prior to rod emergence, demonstrating that oriented motion correlates with local geometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C13 and C136-C139 are supported by fluorescence imaging during recovery shown in Figure 6A-B. The local correlation between shape and MreB orientation, and the transient ring accumulation at bulge necks, provide strong evidence for local geometric sensing.

results.result: Both spheres and rods incorporate new peptidoglycan and wall teichoic acids during rod shape recovery, with WTA ligases diffusing rapidly rather than moving with MreB, indicating that the key difference between rods and spheres is oriented MreB motion rather than differential localization of cell wall components.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C144 are supported by FDAA labeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), ConA staining (Figure 6C), and single-molecule tracking (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-E). The comprehensive analysis of multiple cell wall components strengthens the conclusion that MreB orientation is the primary distinguishing feature.

results.result: The authors propose that MreB functions as a curvature-sensing rudder, with the coupling between filament alignment along greatest principal curvature and shape-reinforcing peptidoglycan synthesis creating a local, self-organizing mechanism for rod shape establishment and maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 and C146-C155, C187-C189 represent the central model synthesizing all experimental findings. The model is well-supported by the convergence of evidence from shape manipulation, confinement, protoplasts, in vitro reconstitution, and modeling. However, some aspects remain speculative regarding the precise molecular mechanisms.

results.result: While circumferential MreB-guided cell wall insertion is expected to reinforce rod shape, it is not sufficient alone, as WTAs working with PG to coordinate Mg2+ and increase cell wall stiffness are also required to maintain rod shape.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C157 are supported by the observation that TagO-depleted cells become round despite having oriented MreB motion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and by the Mg2+ dependence experiments. This appropriately acknowledges the complexity of rod shape maintenance.

results.result: The authors propose that the geometry at bulge-sphere interfaces, which creates regions of negative Gaussian curvature, may nucleate rod formation by focusing MreB filaments into concentrated rings that initiate oriented synthesis, supported by observations of MreB accumulation at bulge necks.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C165 present a mechanistic model for rod nucleation. While the observation of MreB rings at bulge necks (C165, Figure 6B) is well-documented, the detailed geometric mechanism (C160-C164) remains speculative. The model is plausible and supported by modeling (Figure 7B2), but direct experimental validation of the proposed focusing mechanism is lacking.

results.result: The authors propose that MreB enrichment at negative Gaussian curvatures may arise from filaments being steered toward these regions as they move through different curvatures, rather than from differential binding affinities, providing a potential explanation for observed MreB localization patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C169 propose a steering mechanism to explain MreB enrichment patterns. While C166-C167 cite established observations, the steering model (C168-C169) is speculative. The model is consistent with the curvature-sensing mechanism but lacks direct experimental validation.

results.result: The tendency of MreB to align along greatest principal curvature may explain its absence from cell poles, with filaments that enter poles reorienting to move circumferentially upon entering the cell body, as observed by SIM-TIRF microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172 and C174 are supported by SIM-TIRF observations shown in Figure 7C and Movie Figure 7-video 1. The direct visualization of filaments exiting poles and reorienting provides strong evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The authors propose that the slower growth of spherical cells likely arises from downstream effects on cell physiology, such as improper spatial organization of processes like chromosome segregation and division site selection, rather than being mechanistically linked to MreB orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C178 present a reasonable interpretation of the growth rate differences, but the mechanism remains speculative. While C177 cites established knowledge about spatial organization, the causal link to growth rate (C176, C178) is not directly tested.

results.result: The authors propose that MreB filament curvature (200 nm) does not define a specific cell radius (900 nm) but rather acts to orient PG synthesis to maintain or reduce cell diameter, potentially through opposing activities of MreB-associated and non-MreB-associated PG synthases.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C181 present a model for width determination. While the observation about curvature mismatch (C179) is valid, the proposed mechanism (C180-C181) is speculative and not directly tested. The model is plausible but requires further experimental validation.

results.result: Contrary to a previous study, the authors observe directional MreB motion in ΔrodZ E. coli cells across various growth conditions, concluding that directional motion has not been uncoupled from rod shape and that RodZ is not required for directional motion.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C186 address a controversy in the field. The authors' observations (C183-C184) are supported by Figure 7—video 2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. However, the discrepancy with Morgenstein et al. may arise from different imaging conditions, and the conclusions (C185-C186) could benefit from more extensive characterization.

results.result: The manuscript establishes extensive background knowledge about bacterial cell wall structure, peptidoglycan organization, mechanical properties, the Rod complex components, MreB motion characteristics, and wall teichoic acids, drawing from prior literature.
results.evaluation: These claims (C17-C36, C51-C72, C145) represent well-established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. They provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.
